nameStory: The 'dusky' in this sea slug's name comes from its muted, brownish coloration that resembles the dim light of dusk or twilight. Like many sea slugs, it gets its scientific name from a person - in this case, Italian malacologist Salvatore Ercolani who studied Mediterranean mollusks in the 1800s.
description: The Dusky Sea Slug is a tiny marine gastropod that crawls along in shallow coastal waters. These minuscule creatures are typically less than half an inch long, with elongated, flattened bodies that range from brownish-gray to olive-green. Unlike their flashy nudibranch cousins, dusky sea slugs have a more subdued appearance with simple, smooth body shapes. They're part of a group called sacoglossans, which are sometimes nicknamed 'solar-powered sea slugs' for their ability to use stolen plant parts.

idTips.label: Size and Shape
idTips.description: Extremely small - usually under 12mm long - with an elongated, flattened body that feels soft and squishy if gently touched

idTips.label: Coloration
idTips.description: Muted brownish-gray to olive-green color, sometimes with darker speckles, giving it a dusty or faded appearance

idTips.label: Body Structure
idTips.description: Smooth, simple body without the frilly projections or bright colors typical of nudibranchs, with a distinct head region

idTips.label: Habitat Clue
idTips.description: Found crawling on or near green algae, particularly filamentous types, which they pierce and feed on

idTips.label: Movement
idTips.description: Glides smoothly across surfaces leaving a barely visible slime trail, moving much more slowly than you'd expect

habitat: **Note: Information uncertain due to very limited New England records** - Likely found in shallow marine environments such as tide pools, rocky intertidal zones, and protected coves along the coast. These sea slugs typically inhabit areas with abundant green algae growth, particularly on rocks, pier pilings, or in eelgrass beds where their algae food sources thrive.

funFact: **Information uncertain** - Some sea slugs in this family can actually steal chloroplasts from the algae they eat and use them like tiny solar panels to photosynthesize their own food, essentially becoming part plant and part animal!
confusionNotes: **Information uncertain** - Could be confused with other small sea slugs or even tiny marine worms, but the characteristic smooth, flattened body shape and association with green algae helps distinguish it from the more ornate nudibranchs with their colorful projections.
contextualKnowledge: With only 2 recorded observations in New England, this species is either extremely rare in our region or significantly under-observed due to its tiny size and cryptic nature. Many small marine invertebrates like this require careful searching and magnification to spot and identify properly.
compareHints: **Information uncertain** - As the only Ercolania species recorded in our dataset, comparison with other sacoglossan sea slugs would focus on the relatively plain, brownish coloration and small size. Unlike the more colorful Elysia species that might share similar habitats, dusky sea slugs lack the bright greens and elaborate body extensions of their relatives.
